minority governments are less effective than majority governments but are more effective when they are popular.

(1) minority governments are more responsible to the public but less effective in terms of legislative output than majority governments; (2) the responsiveness and effectiveness of minority governments is moderated by their standing in the polls; and (3) the responsiveness and legislative effectiveness of minority governments are positively correlated with each other.
minority governments are both more responsive and less effective than majority governments.

the dynamic factors that condition the trade-off between responsiveness to public opinion and effectiveness in government policy-making.
the conditions under which minority governments can be both responsive and effective.
the conditions under which the trade-off between responsiveness to the public and legislative effectiveness can be overcome.

a minority government is more responsive than a majority government but less effective than a majority government, except when it is popular.
the trade-off between responsiveness to public preferences and effectiveness of legislative output is conditioned by the government status and popularity.

minority government is a good thing if it is popular.

the trade-off between responsiveness to the public and legislative effectiveness is not static, but rather is dynamic and conditioned by minority status and government popularity.
